title: Records, New Orleans and Chicago music reaching New York
summary: Carter and Patrick discuss which records New York musicians heard, from King Oliver to Piron, and New York as a melting pot.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What the word "jazz" means: origins, Dixieland and labels

blocks.x: Let me ask another one which is shifting gears just here a little bit, but what importance would you attach -- especially in the 20's -- to the effect of records and recordings as spreading various styles or influences. I'm thinking here especially of New York, because so many records were made in New York and so many musicians have recounted how influenced they were, how impressed they were by -- especially the Fletcher Henderson records or the early Duke Ellington records which were coming out of New York, but what kind of music came in to New York? What music that was not being played by New York-based groups, was being heard by musicians in New York?
That's a very good question. I'm wondering -- maybe the Dixieland stuff?
Well, that's what I was wondering, too.
Was that coming -- maybe out of Chicago and New Orleans or something?
Well, I'm thinking of the -- what about the King Oliver recordings? Were these very, very popular?
Yes, I think that was coming out of
Well, out of Richmond, Indiana and Gennett# New York and so forth. Jenet and Paramount recordings.
That's right. I think ... was Earl Hines coming out of Indiana or Gennett ... or where was that in Indiana you were saying?
Richmond, Indiana, I guess. We didn't hear too much of Earl Hines until later, after he had gone to join Louis Armstrong, that is.

Uh huh. Well, I'm thinking, or just thinking of things which perhaps are a little bit more of an indigenous jazz style, the King Oliver recordings; the original Dixieland jazz band ... what about A.J. Piron Prong?
He was in New York in 1922 and 1923. Did he have any special impact on you?
Not on me. I don't remember too much about him. I know the name, of course, you know -- but I don't know too much about his music.
And what about ... well, how would you describe the New York scene back then? Because it seems to be such a conglomeration of different kinds of music.
Well, because the musicians, you know, the New York scene was made up of New York musicians plus musicians who, you know, just migrated to New York, like the

'Happy' Caldwells, and Tommy Ladnier, Fletcher Henderson from Cuthbert, Cutpit, Georgia, yes. And gee whiz, it's -- you know -- it was also the melting pot of jazz, you know? New York was ... because of so many musicians from other parts of the country.
